appraisal_events.evidence: les égoïstes ont toujours le dernier mot... leur propre dureté peut aller jusqu'à la plus extrême cruauté sans que cela fasse à leurs yeux qu'aggraver d'autant la culpabilité de l'être assez indélicat pour souffrir, pour avoir raison
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator generalizes from Robert's reproaches against his mother into a pointed analysis of self-justifying egoism, exposing his cruelty toward her as something he recasts as her own fault.

appraisal_events.evidence: d'elle-même Mme de Marsantes cessa d'insister, car elle sentait qu'elle ne le retiendrait plus... je suis sûre que je lui ai fait de la peine... j'aurais voulu le rattraper... pour lui dire que je ne lui en veux pas, que je trouve qu'il a eu raison
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme de Marsantes yields all ground, blames herself for causing him pain, and wants to chase after her son to absolve him, showing her submissive, self-effacing position despite being the wronged party; the narrator's stated pity for her supports this reading.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's maxim about egoists, triggered directly by his conduct, casts Robert as harshly self-justifying toward his mother, clearly lowering his local standing.

She gives up her attempt to keep her son, takes the blame for his distress upon herself, and seeks only to reassure him he was right, showing diminished emotional leverage and self-effacing submission.

ambiguities: Robert de Saint-Loup is never named in this passage; he is identified only via the pronoun 'il' and the address 'maman', resolved through the reference sheet's identification of Mme de Marsantes as his mother.

The narrator's generalization about 'les égoïstes' is phrased as a general maxim rather than a direct statement naming Robert, though it is clearly prompted by and applied to his immediately preceding conduct.
